https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/artic.text: George Russell Mercedes Hungary 'They look very strong' – Russell wary of Ferrari threat in Hungary as Mercedes struggle in Friday practice Ferrari headed both sessions on Friday, while Mercedes failed to show competitive one-lap pace in Hungary. Jul 24, 2026 5:45pm UTC George Russell believes that Ferrari "look very strong" having dominated Friday practice ahead of the Hungarian Grand Prix, while Mercedes struggled for performance. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton each finished fastest in both of Friday's one-hour sessions in Budapest, with the tight, twisty confines of the Hungaroring expected to suit the Scuderia's car this weekend. Despite leading both the Teams' and Drivers' standings, Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli failed to challenge the leading times in either session. "It was quite a strange day out there I think for everybody," said Russell, who finished P5 in both sessions. "It's an amazing track to drive but they've resurfaced half the track, super bumpy. "Our single lap [pace] didn't look great, the long run looked more competitive but what we feared with Ferrari seemed to the case. They look very strong." Russell ended the day only P5 in both sessions Russell admitted that he "trusted in the team that everything has been resolved" after a software issue denied him maximum power at the previous round in Belgium, but that in general "we've got work to do as a team, Ferrari are a good step ahead of everyone right now." Antonelli, who leads Russell by 50 points and Hamilton by 45, had a delayed start to proceedings on Friday, as his Mercedes was being driven by the team's Third Driver Fred Vesti in FP1. Once in the car for FP2, the Italian finished P13 having been unable to complete a Qualifying run, with his first effort halted by a red flag after Franco Colapinto crashed, while he suffered an oversteer moment on his second flying lap. ‘Toughest battle I’ve had psychologically’ – Russell opens up on title fight struggles ahead of Hungarian GP Antonelli struggled to put a flying lap together in FP2 after missing the day's first session Despite the setbacks, Mercedes Deputy Team Principal Bradley Lord was confident the team would be in the mix come Qualifying tomorrow as they look to continue a 100% pole record in Grands Prix this season. "We hope we can fight for pole, we've been competitive at every type of circuit this year," he said. "I know there's a certain narrative that certain circuits favour us and others will favour them. "We've seen generally other teams swing back and forth a reasonable amount but I think we've been pretty consistently fighting up there, at the front and able to compete for pole at every race, so that has to be our target for tomorrow." Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People queue at check-in desks at Heathrow terminal 5 after large-scale disruption caused by an air traffic control system glitch. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty Images Airline industry UK air traffic control problem strands hundreds of thousands of passengers At least 600 flights cancelled as airlines call for overhaul of ATC system after third incident in just over three years UK airport disruption: what are your rights? Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent Tue 8 Sep 2026 14.26 EDT First published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 10.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of thousands of air passengers had flights delayed or cancelled after another UK air traffic control technical glitch kept planes grounded for hours on Tuesday. Airlines demanded action after a “technical issue” at the air traffic control services provider Nats caused the third large-scale stoppage in just over three years. At least 600 flights in and out of the UK were reported cancelled by late Tuesday afternoon in an incident that started at about 1pm and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports, including Heathrow and Gatwick. By the time Nats said it had identified and implemented a fix to restart its flight processing system almost four hours later, most flights scheduled to depart from the London airports and others were yet to take off. The disruption had spread to include incoming flights to much of southern England. Cancellations and delays were continuing well into Tuesday evening, and British Airways said disruption would affect operations through Wednesday at least, with passengers offered free rebooking until Friday. Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed and 50 flights cancelled. The knock-on effects hit flights across Europe, according to easyJet. Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely until the evening. All London airports, as well as Manchester and Birmingham, were among the most directly affected. Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted. According to the flight monitoring website FlightRadar24, easyJet had 137 flights cancelled, British Airways 111, KLM 26, Eurowings 22 and Ryanair 21 by 5pm. View image in fullscreen Passengers stranded at London Gatwick’s south terminal. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA Nats initially announced at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”. It later identified the problem in its flight processing system, and announced at 4.40pm that it had implemented a fix. A spokesperson said the fault was not the same as the ones that caused previous outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025. They said the system was only “starting to recover”. “We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery,” they said. “We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.” The chief executive of Nats, Martin Rolfe, expressed his “huge sympathies to everyone who has been caught up in today’s disruption”. “We absolutely take responsibility for this,” he told Sky News. “We never want this sort of thing to happen. I completely understand how frustrating it is for passengers.” He claims, however, “these things are relatively rare”. “We resolved it to get back to our systems operating normally,” he added. “But of course, there’s a huge amount of disruption that’s now built up in the system. “We’re working very closely now with airlines and airports to try to work through the night to make sure that we can get as many people travelling as possible.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The air traffic control problems follow an “isolated event” a year ago which caused widespread disruption, although it so far appears less severe than the full grounding of flights in August 2023 , which prompted a parliamentary inquiry. However, British Airways said that “the severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact for customers and colleagues”. “We were forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday afternoon, inconveniencing tens of thousands of customers,” a spokesperson said. “This incident was entirely out of our control and incredibly frustrating for our customers and colleagues, with aircraft and crews ending up out of place.” Heathrow originally said only departures had been affected, but a later statement confirmed that the issue was “impacting arriving and departing flights across UK airports”. Airlines renewed calls for Nats to be overhauled after the third incident ascribed to its systems in as many years. Ryanair repeated its calls for Rolfe to resign. The Irish airline’s chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Families travelling on holiday, people travelling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for Nats’ abhorrent failure.” He said the government should “stop making excuses for repeated Nats failures and appoint a new leader capable of running the UK ATC system”. Wizz Air said: “A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. Nats is simply not fit for purpose in its current form.” The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “I’m aware of a technical issue impacting flights at airports including Heathrow and Gatwick. Technicians have identified the issue and are fixing it as we speak. I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry. “I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job.” Explore more on these topics Airline industry Heathrow airport Gatwick airport London Air transport Stansted airport Transport news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story BA boss warns costly aviation taxes and rail tickets are stunting UK growth ‘Inevitable’ jet fuel shortages will drive up air fares this summer, says Willie Walsh Dawn airport drinkers call out Ryanair boss on proposal to ban ‘holiday ritual’ Airlines demand UK relax noise rules and cut flight tax as fuel shortage looms New EU entry-exit system causing up to three-hour delays, say airports Bristol airport loses legal challenge against Cardiff rival over £205m subsidy Flight delays continue across Europe after weekend cyber-attack Air traffic control failure an isolated incident, says UK minister after meeting Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Mud-covered furniture was piled outside homes as people swept thick layers of mud from kitchens and living rooms. Some residents said floodwaters had risen more than 1.5 metres, destroying nearly everything inside their properties. “We can’t use a single thing,” said 56-year-old Candy Vanes, whose home was badly damaged. Emergency crews arrived to assess the destruction as residents faced the task of clearing their homes and salvaging what they could.
